name: Test booster blends (Prime Male, TestoFuel)

card.summary: Multi-herb over-the-counter testosterone-booster products; no published trial of these specific products was found.
card.note: Individual herbal ingredients such as Tribulus have not consistently affected testosterone in controlled studies.

quick.overview:
Test booster blends are over-the-counter supplements that combine several herbs, vitamins and minerals and are marketed to raise or support testosterone. Prime Male and TestoFuel are two brands discussed in these communities.

No published clinical trial of either named product was found. The research that exists concerns individual ingredients, and the sources reviewed describe it as inconsistent.
quick.mechanism: Marketing generally says the ingredients support the body's own testosterone production or reduce its conversion or binding. The sources reviewed do not describe the formulations of either brand, so mechanisms are not assessed here. For one common ingredient, Tribulus terrestris, Wikipedia states that it did not consistently affect testosterone levels in controlled studies [1].
quick.risks: Supplement blends are sold without prior approval for effectiveness. The Australian Institute of Sport, cited by Wikipedia, discourages athletes from using Tribulus supplements, citing no good evidence of effectiveness or safety [1]. Ingredient lists and interactions vary by product.

lead: Test booster blends are multi-ingredient dietary supplements marketed to raise or support testosterone, usually combining herbal extracts, vitamins and minerals. Prime Male and TestoFuel are two brands sold online. People take them hoping for the physique and energy associated with higher testosterone: more muscle, easier training recovery, leaner body composition and better drive in the gym.

The chain users describe is: ingredients nudge the body's own testosterone production or availability, training capacity improves, and muscle gain and leanness follow. Brand formulations are set by the manufacturers and change over time, so the label is the source for ingredients. Common ingredients in this product category include Tribulus terrestris, ashwagandha and fenugreek.

No published clinical trial of Prime Male or TestoFuel as products was found. Wikipedia states that Tribulus did not consistently affect testosterone in controlled studies [1], and its ashwagandha article notes that the herb may raise testosterone levels, with rare reports of liver injury [2].

chain: Herbal and mineral blend taken orally
Claimed support for the body's own testosterone
More muscle, less fat over time
angle.text: Buyers use these blends as a non-prescription way to support testosterone for muscle building and body composition. Brands describe the effect in terms of energy, strength and lean mass.

infobox: Tribulus, ashwagandha, fenugreek, zinc, vitamin D (varies by brand)

paras: Blends differ by brand and product version, so current labels list what each contains. Tribulus terrestris has been used in supplements since the 1980s on the belief that it raises testosterone [1]. Ashwagandha is sold as root or leaf powder or extract [2]. Fenugreek is sold as capsules, powder, tea and extract in many countries [3].

Wikipedia reports that Tribulus did not consistently affect testosterone in controlled studies and that no reviews show strength-enhancing effects [1]. Its ashwagandha article says the herb may raise testosterone, which could matter for people on certain cancer medicines [2]. Its fenugreek article describes studies as mostly small and of limited quality and says the US FDA has not approved fenugreek for clinical use [3].

Ashwagandha has been linked to rare herb-induced liver injury, most often in people with existing liver conditions, plus diarrhea, headache, sedation and nausea; it is advised against in pregnancy and hormone-sensitive prostate cancer [2]. Fenugreek can cause digestive upset, a maple-like body odor and low blood sugar, and may interact with diabetes and anticoagulant drugs [3]. The Australian Institute of Sport discourages athletes from using Tribulus supplements [1].
No studies found of Prime Male or TestoFuel as products.
Ingredient-level research, as summarised by Wikipedia, is inconsistent for Tribulus [1] and limited in quality for fenugreek [3].

Testosterone-focused forums such as T Nation discuss test boosters often. One member who used a mild booster reported worse sleep, which surprised him since zinc is a common ingredient [4]. Another posted lab results after stopping boosters and adding vitamin D and boron, reporting lower total and free testosterone [5]. Others ask whether any boosters work [6]. Such posts are individual reports.

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, test boosters are discussed both as a first step before prescription therapy and as something members question.

claims.claim: Over-the-counter test boosters raise testosterone enough to help muscle gain.
claims.believers: Users report feeling better or stronger on boosters and some post lab changes when they stop or start supplements [5][7].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says Tribulus did not consistently affect testosterone in controlled studies [1]; ashwagandha may raise it [2]; no trial of the named blends was found.

claims.claim: Boosters made from common ingredients such as zinc improve sleep and recovery.
claims.believers: The expectation is that zinc and similar minerals aid both testosterone and sleep.
claims.experts: A forum user who tried boosters reported worse sleep instead [4]; no study of the branded products was found.
